Excuse
eks-kūz´
n., v. (a plea offered to avoid; rendering Greek paraiteomai and anapologetos)
From Latin excusare, to free from a charge. An excuse is an offered reason — and Scripture examines several and accepts none.

Biblical Definition

An excuse is a plea to be released. Christ's parable records three in a row: “they all with one consent began to make excuse” — a field, five yoke of oxen, and a wife (Luk 14:18–20). Paul says creation leaves men “without excuse” (Rom 1:20), and again of the moralizer, “therefore thou art inexcusable, O man” (Rom 2:1). Adam's first response to God is an excuse that implicates both his wife and his Maker (Gen 3:12).

Webster 1828 Definition

Webster (1828) defines excuse as a plea offered in extenuation of a fault or irregular deportment; apology; and that which excuses, that which extenuates or justifies a fault.

expand to see more

EXCUSE, v.t. To pardon; to free from the imputation of fault or blame; to acquit of guilt.

2. To pardon, as a fault; to forgive entirely, or to admit to be little censurable.

3. To free from an obligation or duty.

EXCUSE, n. A plea offered in extenuation of a fault or irregular deportment; apology.

Key Scripture

Luk 14:18 — "And they all with one consent began to make excuse. The first said unto him, I have bought a piece of ground, and I must needs go and see it: I pray thee have me excused."

Rom 1:20 — "For the invisible things of him from the creation of the world are clearly seen, being understood by the things that are made, even his eternal power and Godhead; so that they are without excuse:"

Rom 2:1 — "Therefore thou art inexcusable, O man, whosoever thou art that judgest: for wherein thou judgest another, thou condemnest thyself; for thou that judgest doest the same things."

Gen 3:12 — "And the man said, The woman whom thou gavest to be with me, she gave me of the tree, and I did eat."

Modern Corruption

Excuses are offered as though sincerity settled the matter, and every excuse in Luke 14 was true, reasonable, and fatal.

expand to see more

Luke 14:18-20 is careful to make the excuses good ones. A purchased field must be inspected; new oxen must be proved; a newly married man had a legal exemption from military service. None of the three is a lie, and none of them is trivial. That is what makes the parable so uncomfortable — the invitation was declined by reasonable men with genuine commitments, and the master's response was anger and a guest list drawn from the streets.

Genesis 3:12 records the first excuse ever offered and its structure has not improved since: the woman whom thou gavest to be with me, she gave me of the tree, and I did eat. Two parties are implicated before the confession arrives, and the confession itself is three words long. Adam's answer is technically accurate in every particular, which is precisely why Scripture treats accuracy as an insufficient defence.

Greek & Hebrew Roots

Greek paraiteomai (G3868), to beg off, excuse oneself; anapologetos (G379), without excuse, indefensible.

expand to see more

Greek paraiteomai (G3868) — to make excuse, beg off; Luke 14:18-19.

Greek anapologetos (G379) — without excuse; Romans 1:20, 2:1.

Greek prophasis (G4392) — a pretext, cloke; John 15:22, now they have no cloke for their sin.

Usage

"“They all with one consent began to make excuse” — three good reasons, all fatal."

"“So that they are without excuse” — the verdict on creation's testimony."

"“The woman whom thou gavest to be with me” — the first excuse, technically accurate."
